speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In recent days, members of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers have been engaging in work stoppages in various parts of the country, including St. John's, Newfoundland, yesterday, protesting various violations of the current contract. That compliments exactly the deceit of the right hon. gentleman in appearing to imply here in the House .. .
The use of unparliamentary language is a practice that has long been held to be disorder in the House. The attitude of the Chair is that, when in doubt in terms of the interpretation of a term, it is always best to err on the side of asking an hon. member who has used language in the heat of the moment to withdraw it in order to uphold the dignity of the practices of the House.
In this particular case it may give the House some indication of the difficulty in these particular matters to say that in examining the precedents, in preparation for having to make a decision on this matter, it comes down to so fine a distinction as a situation in the past when the word "deception" was used, and was held and defended as not being an unparliamentary word. The question, therefore, becomes: is there sufficient distinction between the word "deception" and the word "deceit" to permit the one and disallow the other? In my considered opinion, upon examining dictionary definitions ordinarily attributed to the use of the word "deceit", that is so. The word "deception" does not have the same connotation as the word "deceit".
"Deceit" is ordinarily defined as follows:
The action or practice of deceiving; concealment of the truth in order to mislead; deception, fraud, cheating.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I should like at third reading to deal with a number of major themes which were raised in the debate on second reading, and which also ran through a number of questions raised during committee stage. First may I express my appreciation to the Chairman, the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik), and members of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs for the care and attention they devoted to the study of the bill and their promptness in reporting, which has made it easier to bring this bill forward in the tight time frame we face.
I suppose if one reads the reports of debates on the bill, and committee proceedings, one cannot help but be impressed by the quality of ambivalence in many of the statements made not only by the opposition but made by myself, as well, and others in the course of discussions. There is a quality of ambivalence because, on the one hand, there has been an effort on the part of those dealing with the bill to take a further step which would reinforce provincial autonomy, reinforce the autonomy of the provincial governments or, to use a current buzzword, further the cause of decentralization. But there has been, at the same time, support for the continuing role of the federal government in providing financial support for provincial governments in essential services, particularly for provincial governments with a smaller than average tax base. I do not think anyone needs to apologize for this ambivalence. They are both desirable and legitimate goals, and many of our federal-provincial relations in this area, those to do with this bill and those established over the years, have been attempts to arrive at some kind of balance between those two forces.
The bill, in my opinion, does that, I think quite successfully. That is not to say that it could not be improved upon in terms of balance or of division of responsibilities as between the two levels of government; but it does represent the result of a concerned and careful effort on all sides to arrive at an appropriate sharing of revenue and an appropriate sharing of responsibility, in order to make certain that these essential public services continue to be provided.

speechtext:
I propose to go on with my speech and let the minister think through the implications of what he is asking me to do.
What I was saying is that it is most unfair and unjust to expect the Parliament of Canada to ratify a bill which affects native peoples or anybody else, without having the opportunity to make any input into the measure. That is what I was saying.
I recognize it is an extremely difficult situation. What I was trying to discuss, if the minister were not so impatient, is the difficulty parliament experiences when it is faced with a bill the parameters of which are already drawn. That is all.
Without being overly immodest, I believe some people in this House do possess a degree of insight into at least two or three of the concerns dealt with in this bill. I said earlier that these insights come to us because of the manner in which we carry out our responsibilities as members. I happen to have made it my business to understand the issues surrounding post-secondary education, and I will come to that aspect later, but first I should like to talk about health care because the people and the government of New Brunswick are anxious about health care.
It is a fact that by November, 1976, the proposal for the funding of extended health care service had become, from Canada's point of view, an appendage to the established program financing proposal rather than a separate cost-sharing issue in the health field. This, as the minister of health said, amounted to a fundamental change of direction which took place between April, 1976, and November, 1976, I think it was. I am not criticizing this. I am saying that in the long discussions which went on it was not until November that the change took place. The November date was the climax of meetings between ministers of health, meetings with officials, and then the meeting of first ministers beginning in April, 1976. All this culminated in a revised plan for health care offered by Canada on the basis that a decision had to be made by February 15, 1977, or, as the minister's statement went, block funding would lapse. Those were the terms of the deadline.
I do not wish to appear to be confining this appeal solely to the concern of one province, but the anxiety of New Brunswick is symptomatic of something larger than the preoccupation of one particular province. In fact it goes to the core of the federal government's perception of its role in the partnership. New Brunswick shares the objective of controlling the rate of cost increase for existing programs and of developing lower cost alternative programs which are more humane in their application to the people who need them.
My province believes that the application of block funding to extended health care programs is not appropriate at this time because of the nature of the services covered by the block funding concept. The concept itself is good and logical when applied to mature services, but it is inconsistent with the encouragement of basic health services which are similar throughout Canada because New Brunswick has not reached a sufficiently advanced stage in health service development. This is a perfect illustration of the dilemma in which one finds

oneself when trying to develop programs which are strictly the same from one part of the country to another, that is, the same in terms of money.
Hospital insurance and medical care are reasonably consistent across Canada. I believe the government is to be congratulated upon this, as are the provincial governments. There is consistency across the country. So block funding in itself is not the problem. The rub comes in the field of extended health care. There is a very great variety in the quality and kinds of services available in hospitals across the country. I have to say that in New Brunswick the system is, at this stage, immature. Growth is under way, but time is needed until the services are fully developed.
The province of New Brunswick had asked for a very modest concession during a transitional period so that hardship might be avoided. The minister turned down that request. When I last spoke to him about it in committee, he said to me that he had not even responded to a letter from the province, stating reasons for declining the suggestion. The request by the province was a modest one seeking a transitional amount of $6 million in descending sums over the next three years. This is what was proposed to the minister of health. The province would accept the block funding concept but would prefer a phase-out period of three years.
The minister told us in committee that this was impossible. He spoke of federal funds as being gravy-that was the word he used-and said the provinces should not expect "more gravy". I should like the minister to name any one of the four Atlantic provinces which is on some sort of "gravy train" as far as health care programs or any other of these services are concerned. I suggest such an attitude makes "co-operative federalism" sound hollow and that the newest cliche which is being trotted out, flexible federalism, will prove no better if, when there is an opportunity to bring some flexibility to the concept, the government turns it down the first time it is tested.
I have two compliments to pay. One is to my colleague, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) who really did a superior job in analysing this bill and studying it through the committee stage. She warned us of some of the dangers, one or two of which I have noted. One is the lack of any review mechanism, and also the danger inherent if we are not perfectly sure that there will be some sort of equality across the country in the service area.
It is interesting and very positive that one of the other women in public life is Judith Maxwell. I suppose "public life" is not the phrase to use about Judith Maxwell, but surely outside parliament Judith Maxwell must be one of the most interesting women commenting on Canada today. In "Policy Review and Outlook, 1977" she discusses an agenda for change. In a small paragraph on page 8 of that booklet she suggests:
The structural questions outlined here are an agenda for personal reflection as much as they are for government action, for the individual will be facing two
March 23, 1977

challenges in the next few years. First, it is important for individual Canadians to understand that there are powerful forces at work which will inevitably alter the status quo.
Of course the status quo is being altered, I think for the best in general terms, by the bill which we are' now debating at third reading stage. But I do worry about the health care provisions, I do worry about the lack of mechanisms, and I worry particularly about the whole aspect of post-secondary education. The minister did refer to this concern in his speech a minute or two ago.
Claude Bissell, the former president of the University of Toronto, wrote a lively book called "Half-way up Parnassus". When this bill was being debated I could not help but think that this minister-or perhaps this is being unfair to him and I should confine this to the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) under whose aegis post-secondary education comes-could write a book called "Descending Parnassus" because there is no doubt that under the provisions of this bill the Government of Canada, not in dollar terms but in terms of its concern for its undoubted obligation, role, and responsibility in postsecondary education, is changing direction, is, as I say, descending Parnassus.
The bill has a political element in the funding arrangements. The government, as a matter of fact, in another area has said that it has reduced over-all spending by 2.4 per cent, thereby gaining, I presume, some political brownie points. But in an article in the April edition of University Affairs which, by happy coincidence came just yesterday, in a feature article by Lynda Woodcock, concern was expressed about increasing provincial control. It reads:
Increasing provincial control over all aspects of post-secondary education was a major topic of discussion at a recent conference on higher education held at the university of Manitoba.
The conference was sponsored by Manitoba's education faculty as a contribution to the university's celebration of its centennial.
Two other important topics considered at length were university-government relations and university governance-
Then there follows a discussion by Dr. Claude Thibault, who is the executive director of the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada. The article reads:
Dr. Thibault noted that the federal government's attempt to have some influence on post-secondary policies had failed.
Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau had recommended that a permanent policy forum for the federal and provincial governments be set up for discussion on post-secondary matters. This idea was rejected by the provinces.
Surely that is not good enough. If the idea was rejected by the provinces, the leadership of this government was at stake. I have no doubt in the world that there is a constitutional imperative for the federal government in post-secondary education to continue to play its national role, and it concerns me deeply that by changing some of the financial formulas we could be in danger of increasing provincial control. I think that is a matter that should concern all of us in the Parliament of Canada who are federalists.

Mr. Speaker, before I get to the substance of my comments in third reading debate I would like to raise and dispose of some misinforma-
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements tion provided by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) in the House, and deal with the opening comments of the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather).
In his comments this afternoon the minister said that I had misinformed the House when I said that the provinces were not happy with this agreement, that they did not accept it. I would like to refer the minister to the transcript. It was a closed session but I obtained copies of the transcript of the first ministers' meeting of December 14, 1976, when premier Lougheed replied to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on behalf of all the provinces in response to the specific set of proposals that we are debating in the House this afternoon. Here is what premier Lougheed said on behalf of the provinces:
... all the provinces are of the view that the proposal... is inadequate, but a number of provinces felt they were left with no alternative but to accept it.
It was inadequate, but they had to accept it. Why did they accept it? They accepted it for the obvious reason that, as the Minister of Finance in his quiet and reasonable way indicated, the ultimate authority rests with the Parliament of Canada. The existing agreements were due to be terminated on March 31 of this year and the provinces had to take what they could get. They had to like it or lump it. When they got this set of inequitable proposals put before them-of course they contained some crumbs, particularly for the poorer provinces, with which they were pleased in the short run-rather than being left with nothing at all after March 31 they accepted the package. But to imply, as the minister did, that this is something they all entered into voluntarily, that there was a happy round of cheers on the part of the premiers, is just .absurd. It was forced upon them. It was federal legislation. They had no alternative. So I stand by what I said in the'House when we debated second reading on February 18. This was not an agreement reached on a voluntary basis by the provinces.
The second point I would like to make before getting on to the substance of my comments is that the hon. member for Fundy-Royal said that I seemed to be huffing and puffing a bit today, and he could not quite understand it. My own view is that when you have something to huff and puff about, if you are prepared to take a stand on an issue which you think is important and relevant, then it is appropriate to show that with a little emotional concern as well as with arguments to support your position.

At that time the New Democratic Party argued for precisely that course of action, and we argued that the serious inequalities that existed between our provinces had to be removed. We argued that all the provinces east of the Ottawa River had a very real difficulty ensuring that kids growing up in that part of Canada-in half the provinces of Canada-had the same opportunities and expectations as kids growing up elsewhere in this country.
What was embarked upon in the 1960's is now being systematically destroyed by the Prime Minister of Canada, with the total support of the Conservative party. The leader of the Conservative party (Mr. Clark) at second reading supported the principle of this legislation. What is at stake is the abolition of national programs, the justification for which was to equalize conditions across the country.

The point I am making is that when we are in the process of transferring tax points to the provinces and saying to the provinces that in the long run they will have to finance hospitals, medical services, and university educations for their kids, that is exactly like saying that under Canadian law rich men and poor men all have the same right to buy a Cadillac. That is exactly what is involved, and it is no coincidence that in the real world the keys for the Cadillac always end up in the pockets of the rich.
As I said earlier, in this process there is an abandonment of the program which was established by the former prime minister of this country, Lester Pearson. I made the point in the second reading debate that this bill is harmful to Canada because a person growing up on Cape Breton Island ought to have the same opportunities in basic aspects of existence not only as another person growing up in Halifax, in that same province, but the same opportunity as a cousin who may live in Calgary or someone who may live in downtown Toronto.
If a common sense of nationhood means anything, we must establish basic common conditions all across this land. That was what was involved in the 1960's when we were developing important national programs, but we are now destroying that structure. That is harmful in terms of equality, and particularly at this particular time in our history it is harmful in terms of national unity. The two go together because in order for men, women and children in one part of Canada-whether it is in the Gaspe region of Quebec or in the province of Newfoundland, which is one vast area of unemployment, or in Victoria or in Moose Jaw-to develop a sense of commonality and iden-

tification with the national government, they have to sense that there is now in existence either a basic state of equality in Canada, or at least that government programs are moving toward the establishment of a state of equality in certain basic respects.

speechtext:
We are now moving in precisely the opposite direction. We are now saying that people who grow up in Alberta, British Columbia, and Ontario are going to have greater opportunities-even greater than they now have-and greater expectations in life for themselves and their families than people growing up in other parts of the country. That is not only wrong from the point of view of equality, but it is also fundamentally wrong at this point in our history on the part of a government which ought to be concerned about the question of national unity.
I predict that-not next year or the year after, perhaps in the third year, but certainly by the fifth year-this program will bring about a worsening of the economic position of Atlantic Canada and of the province of Quebec compared with the rest of Canada. What that means is that there will be more resentment. The east and the west will be in greater conflict. English Canadians will be less prepared than they are now to accept the aspirations of the people of the province of Quebec. In short, with this technical legislation we are sowing the seeds of grievous discontent.
My party believes that the issues at stake are very serious. The right alternative to some provincial dissatisfaction with existing federal-provincial agreements in post-secondary education, in medicare, and in hospitalization is not to move toward the shifting of tax point power to the provinces which, as I said, favours the rich over the poor, nor is to be found in a similar proposal which is discussed these days by the Conservative party of Canada and in some Liberal circles, which is to transfer constitutional power more specifically and clearly back to the provinces and to make sure that the provinces stay narrowly within those rigid confines. Neither of those approaches is favoured by my party.
What the New Democratic Party says is required at this time is the maintenance of effective national programs. This will ensure a basic state of equality in the health and education fields across the country. We need programs for medical care, health, and education, programs that will ensure a state of equity across Canada, but programs that will be flexible in terms of administrative decentralization. There is no reason why we cannot take the rhetoric of decentralization seriously and apply it within the framework of national programs.
We could have a department of national housing, which we should have, to allocate substantial amounts of money for housing to the provinces on an equalized basis. That would not mean we would need a body such as Central Mortgage and Housing to lay down rigorous standards for housing in British
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Columbia, for instance, where requirements are different from those in Ontario, or different from the architectural and traditional requirements of Quebec. We could have a national program on housing which would say to the provinces, "Here is the money which we raised on a national basis because that removes some of the inequities that exist between the provinces. All you have to do is spend so much of it within a broad income category to make sure it goes to low and medium income Canadians first." There could perhaps be ceilings on the prices of houses, but that is all. The provinces would meet their own architectural traditions and geographic circumstances. Taking the decentralization rhetoric seriously, this would allow the provinces to do a good job on housing.
A similar proposition could be put in the medical care and hospitalization fields. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), backed by the Prime Minister, insisted that all provinces in order to get money for hospitalization had to build acute care hospitals that just did not make either medical or economic sense. Instead of abolishing the program, and instead of the federal government getting out entirely, all that was needed was for the government to lay down broad guidelines for the provinces, saying in effect that it is important for money to be spent on hospitalization from British Columbia to New Brunswick but that the provinces should decide whether it should go, say, for nursing homes or acute care hospitals. The federal government does not know the details of provincial requirements, but the provincial governments do, and they should be allowed to decide the appropriate priorities for spending in such fields.
I could select other examples, Mr. Speaker, but those two will suffice. We need national programs in these areas now as never before in our history because of the value of equality in itself but in particular because of the need to generate support from one coast to the other for the national government-the need to show Canadians, wherever they live, that there is a national government that cares what happens to them. We are not getting such an indication from this government. The road we are embarked upon with this legislation indicates just the opposite; we are going to see the rich provinces getting richer and more powerful, and the poor provinces getting poorer and less powerful. That leads to less of a sense of Canadian identity and less sense of commitment to the national government, but to a greater sense of regional identification and more regional antagonism. We believe that is the wrong direction.
This bill ought to be opposed, Mr. Speaker. It ought not to have been introduced. All of us in this House who believe in national unity, who believe in equality of opportunity, ought to vote against it.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on this bill, and particularly on the aspect of returning more control over health and welfare programs to the provinces. The Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent), who just spoke, laid great emphasis on national programs and national unity, but we have never had greater national disunity than since these programs were introduced. I

March 23, 1977
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements
have long maintained that one cause of dissatisfaction among Canadians has been the fact that the federal government has undertaken responsibility for programs of health and welfare, and also of education. The object was to promote national unity, but in fact the opposite has been the case.
Up until 20 or so years ago most communities looked after their own medical care, hospital care, and education up to university level, and they did not do too badly. There is no evidence that in different parts of Canada the incidence of death was higher, the incidence of disease was greater, or that the incidence of morbidity was any greater in one area than in another. There is no evidence of that in the United States either where the social structure is somewhat similar.
In the 1960's the Pearson government decided that the federal government should oversee the health of the citizens of Canada; that provincial governments were not to be trusted to look after their citizens. That was a great mistake, Mr. Speaker. Unfortunately most of the extra money allocated for the purpose vanished into brick and concrete, or costly administration.
I think it is important that the provinces have the right to administer their own health and welfare programs and, even more important, that the municipal governments should share in the administration. I think it behooves us to look at the possibility of such things as property tax deductions for residential areas. This would encourage local governments to assume some responsibility for health costs in the form of hospitals, diagnostic clinics, and so on.
I think it is significant that the greatest trend toward national disunity has occurred since the federal government has assumed control of collecting the vast amounts of money needed to run the three programs. That is now being returned to the provinces to be spent on programs that are rather restrictive and often unsuitable for the particular province involved.
I think the federal government, in essence, bypassed the provinces by assuming the problems of health, welfare and education. It raised the money through the tax system, and so effectively bypassed the provinces and prevented them from meeting their obligations.
The provinces should have the right to decide whether their money is invested in hospitals, medical care, and post-secondary educational institutions, and they should have some leeway in this. Obviously there would be a difference in standards between provinces and we would have to make allowances for that.
In spite of all this, Mr. Speaker, I think this legislation is a step along the way. I think it will increase our national well-being in the long run even though its application may at times create some inequities.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977   MEASURE FOR MAKING CERTAIN FISCAL PAYMENTS AND OF ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall comment briefly on the remarks of the hon. member for

Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie) and of the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather).
It seems to me that when the hon. member for Dauphin said we should go back to the good old days when hospital care was a matter for local communities, he forgot that, in those days, many small communities were without doctors and many Canadians could not pay their doctors' bills. Often people could not enter hospital, or, if they did, could not pay the hospital bill and saw liens placed against their houses.
The hon. member forgets that a Conservative government, led by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker), put into effect a hospital insurance plan when it participated with one province in the cost-sharing of hospitalization. That led to all provinces joining the hospitalization plan. The royal commission appointed by that right hon. gentleman produced a report which led to the establishment in all provinces of a health insurance plan jointly funded by the federal and provincial governments.
Why was I not in attendance in the committee when it dealt with this bill? As my leader has already said, the answer partly is that at the same time I was serving on another committee. But the other reason is that I had participated in the debate on the bill. We had made our position clear, indicated that in our opinion the bill would have disastrous effects on national unity and on standards of service provided from one end of the country to the other.
We heard that the Conservative party intends to support the bill. I am not surprised that Conservative members from Ontario or Alberta support this bill. Those provinces stand to gain. They will get more dollars under this bill than under the old arrangement. As well, those two provinces are best able to carry the burden once the federal government withdraws from shared cost programs. The other provinces, New Brunswick, the province of the hon. member for Fundy-Royal, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, and Manitoba will find it much more difficult to bear the heavier costs once the federal government's plan either to withdraw from or reduce its share of shared-cost programs comes into effect.
The hon. member for Fundy-Royal told the House this bill will have adverse effects in New Brunswick. Having said that, he turned around and said he would vote for the bill. I knew the Conservatives would not oppose the bill, and because I knew the bill would come back from committee virtually unchanged, or as it had been sent to committee, I decided to attend another meeting.
What will happen as a result of changes to the Medical Care Act, and the federal government's announcement that as soon as it legally can it will cut back its 50 per cent contribution under hospital insurance? The result will be obvious. As the government reduces spending on health, medical insurance, hospital insurance, and post-secondary education, the have-not provinces will be forced to pay the extra cost. They already have the highest tax rates in the country and, some of them, the highest sales tax rates in the country. They will be forced to increase taxes, to introduce fees as a deterrent, to increase university enrollment and tuition fees, or reduce services.
March 23, 1977

For many years we thought that one of the benefits of being a Canadian was that, no matter if one lived in Newfoundland or Vancouver Island, one was entitled to the same basic services. That meant Canadians did not have to worry about paying hospital bills, among other things. I am sure hon. members have heard of Canadian citizens unfortunate enough to be sick in the United States and forced to pay hospital bills in the United States. Those bills can run to several thousand dollars for two or three weeks of hospital care. Even Canadians not in lower income brackets would find it difficult to pay such bills. The experience of Canadians forced to see doctors in the United States is similar. The United States, the wealthiest country in the world, is the only industrialized country without a hospital insurance plan and without a medical insurance plan. Is there a member here who thinks we should do without these plans?

speechtext:
I do not say our plans are perfect. Partly, we oppose this bill because several provinces, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Prince Edward Island and Quebec, think certain services can be provided more cheaply and efficiently outside intensive care hospitals which are jointly funded by the federal government. Unfortunately those outside services are not funded by the federal government. The bill makes no provision in this regard, and that is partly why we think it is wrong. It will reduce minimum health service standards and the availability of post-secondary education which, so far, we have been able to provide to Canadians in all parts of Canada.
This year, pretty well every university raised its student enrollment fees. Now, since Ottawa is to cut back the proportion of money it makes available for university education, our universities must increase fees once more. As well, most provinces will face severe financial constraints. For those reasons we oppose the bill, as we opposed the change in the Medical Care Act. We shall oppose any changes to the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. We oppose this kind of whittling away of basic and fundamental rights all Canadians have enjoyed for a quarter of a century. This whittling away can only aid the cause of separatists in all parts of the country, Quebec, Alberta or British Columbia.
If you cut back services, how can you make people believe it is great to be Canadian? Why should people in New Brunswick enjoy a lower level of service than people in Ontario and British Columbia? Because the people of Ontario or British Columbia live in provinces with resources fetching high prices now, surely that does not entitle them to infinitely better services than are available to people in Newfoundland or New Brunswick? That, fundamentally, is why we oppose this bill.
I do not want to repeat what I said at the second reading stage of the bill. However, I want to dispute vigorously the statement made today by the Minister of Finance, as well as the statements made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) when we were debating this bill on
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements second reading, that the provinces voluntarily accepted this bill, that they welcomed this bill, and that they will be better off as a result of it. The facts are, as our leader put on the record, that the premier of Alberta, speaking on behalf of all the provinces, made it clear to the federal government that all ten provincial governments, regardless of party, were opposed to the provisions of this bill.
The minister said that the provinces have accepted the bill. He implies that we are not telling the truth. Of course they accepted the bill. They knew that if they did not accept it, the funding which they have been getting for these programs under the old legislation would end. It had a time limit. They would not be entitled to any funding when the legislation would end this month. They had a choice between accepting this bill or getting nothing, because there would be no legislation in effect. They would have to depend on the charity and good will of the federal government. And they had sufficient experience with this federal government to realize that they did not want to be put in that position.
Let me point out what will happen to the provinces as a result of the passage of this bill. The province of Ontario will get $50 million in the next fiscal year, British Columbia will get $23 million, and Alberta $90 million. The poorer provinces stand to lose. Prince Edward Island will lose $2 million. Saskatchewan will lose up to $3 million. Manitoba will gain $800,000 the first year, but will lose money in subsequent years. That is only with respect to alternate care for adults who can be placed in institutions other than intensive care hospital beds.
The minister must not be permitted to get away with his statement that the provincial governments not only accepted this bill but will in fact be better off than they would have been had the bill not been passed. I want to put on the record the views of the two provincial governments with which we are in closest contact. I am sure that if the hon. member for Fundy-Royal had asked the government of New Brunswick for its analysis, he would have received approximately the same information as we got from Saskatchewan and Manitoba.
I would like to quote what the minister of finance in Manitoba said at the meeting of ministers of finance held February 1 and 2, 1977. With regard to this whole question of the federal government's per capita offer for extended health care services he said, and I quote:
Up to now, our assessment of the proposals in their ever-changing form is that they are not an adequate replacement for cost sharing commitments which had previously been made by the federal government. Our own calculations suggest that the per capita amounts offered so far would barely offset existing recoveries for Manitoba. And, they would not come close to matching the support levels that were anticipated under:
The 1975 offer to extend hospital and medical care sharing to cover alternative services, and the mid-1976 version of the proposed social services act.
Let me stop quoting for a moment to say to the minister that that social services act was not proposed by some government that had no experience and did not know of the implications of the proposals. It was proposed by this federal Liberal government less than a year ago.
